content: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is an infection of the lungs that develops outside of hospital settings. It is the most prevalent form of pneumonia and a significant cause of both illness and death. Common symptoms include difficulty breathing, fever, chest pain, and coughing. The causative agents of CAP include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. Diagnosis can often be made based on clinical symptoms and physical examination, but additional tests such as chest X-rays, sputum analysis, and other laboratory investigations are frequently employed. Treatment primarily involves the use of antibiotics, and certain forms of CAP can be prevented through vaccination. Historically, Sir William Osler, often referred to as the Father of Modern Medicine, recognized the severity of pneumonia, calling it the Captain of the Men of Death in 1918. However, advancements in the 20th century, such as the introduction of penicillin, other antibiotics, modern surgical techniques, and intensive care, significantly reduced pneumonia-related mortality in developed countries. Vaccination efforts, such as those against Haemophilus influenzae type b (initiated in 1988) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (introduced for adults in 1977 and for children in 2000), have led to dramatic declines in cases. The lower respiratory tract is protected by various pulmonary defense mechanisms. CAP occurs when these defenses are breached or when there is an overwhelming exposure to virulent infectious agents. Transmission can occur through aspiration (macro or micro), circulation, local spread, traumatic inoculation, or iatrogenic means. Impaired immunity and the inability to filter out pathogens increase the risk of developing pneumonia. The causative organisms vary depending on factors such as age, immune status, geographic location, and comorbid conditions. CAP can be caused by viral, bacterial, or fungal pathogens. The most common cause in adult outpatients and inpatients is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Patients admitted to intensive care units often have infections caused by more aggressive organisms, such as Staphylococcus aureus or Gram-negative bacilli. Neonates are particularly susceptible to Group B Streptococcus (GBS), which accounts for approximately 50% of pneumonias in the first week of life. Children and elderly individuals are more prone to viral infections and atypical bacterial pneumonias caused by organisms like Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, and Legionella. Pneumonia must be differentiated from other non-infectious conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as interstitial lung disease, congestive heart failure (CHF), cancer, and pulmonary embolism. Globally, pneumonia is the leading cause of death in children under five years of age. Both children and the elderly are at higher risk of complications from pneumonia, and mortality rates are higher in children from developing countries. Risk factors for pneumonia include smoking, advanced age, immunosuppression, exposure to chemicals, and underlying lung diseases. Complications of pneumonia, such as sepsis, respiratory failure, pleural effusion, and empyema, can occur even with appropriate antibiotic treatment. Bacterial pneumonia is more frequently associated with complications than viral pneumonia. Most bacterial pneumonias can be resolved within one to two weeks with proper treatment, while viral pneumonias may take longer, and mycoplasmal pneumonias may require four to six weeks for complete resolution. The prognosis depends on the severity of the illness at the time of diagnosis. The CURB-65 score is a validated clinical tool used to predict mortality in CAP and infections at other sites. It is recommended by the British Thoracic Society for assessing the severity of pneumonia. Another tool, the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI), helps clinicians estimate the probability of morbidity and mortality in CAP patients. Common symptoms of pneumonia include cough, fever, and difficulty breathing. Patients with CAP often report close contact with others exhibiting similar symptoms. Physical examination may reveal fever or, in some cases, hypothermia, increased respiratory rate, low blood pressure, tachycardia, or low oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry or blood gas analysis. Patients with severe symptoms, such as respiratory distress, confusion, or cyanosis (bluish skin), require immediate medical attention. Abnormal breath sounds, crackles (rales), or increased loudness of whispered speech (whispered pectoriloquy) may indicate areas of lung consolidation, where the lung tissue is stiff and filled with fluid. Palpation and percussion of the chest can help localize these areas, and increased tactile fremitus (vibrations felt on the chest during speech) may also be detected. Laboratory findings, such as leukocytosis, can aid in diagnosing bacterial pneumonia and assessing the patient’s condition. Sputum samples should be collected for Gram staining and culture to identify the specific pathogen causing the pneumonia. Additional tests include urine antigen testing, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and procalcitonin levels. Chest X-rays are a critical diagnostic tool for pneumonia, revealing areas of opacity (appearing white) that represent consolidation. However, pneumonia may not always be visible on X-rays, especially in its early stages or if it involves parts of the lung that are difficult to visualize. Chest CT scans are not routinely performed but can be useful when X-ray findings are inconclusive. CT findings may include lobar consolidation, ground-glass opacities, pleural effusion, lymphadenopathy, and a tree-in-bud appearance. Ultrasound can also be used in certain cases to diagnose and monitor pneumonia, guide thoracocentesis, and quantify pleural effusion. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) can help identify uncommon pathogens causing CAP and assist in differentiating infectious from non-infectious pneumonia. Treatment of CAP involves the use of appropriate antibiotics and management of complications. Empirical therapy may be initiated while awaiting culture results, and once the results are available, treatment can be tailored to the specific pathogen. Empirical therapy is guided by severity assessments using tools like the PSI and CURB-65 score and typically includes coverage for both typical and atypical bacteria. Primary prevention strategies for infectious pneumonia include treating underlying illnesses (e.g., AIDS), smoking cessation, and vaccination against pneumococcal and influenza pathogens.
